title: Downtown Denver
name: Downtown Denver
metaTitle: Downtown Denver 1031 Exchange Services | 1031 Exchange Denver
metaDescription: Downtown Denver 1031 exchange guidance for high-rise office, government-leased buildings, and 16th Street Mall retail in the Denver central business district.

sections.html: Downtown Denver is the high-rise core, 17th Street towers, government buildings, banks, and the 16th Street Mall running through the middle of it. It is the oldest commercial stock in the metro, and it trades on a different set of rules than the suburban product on the rest of this identification list.

sections.heading: The Office Stock on 17th Street
sections.html:
Most of the towers along 17th Street and Broadway went up between the 1970s oil boom and the early 2000s. A handful of Class A buildings still lease well to law firms, energy companies, and government agencies. A lot of the Class B and C stock behind them has sat with real vacancy since 2020, and that gap is exactly why some of it now trades as a value-add or conversion play instead of a stabilized office hold.

Floor plates in the older towers run deep and narrow, which matters if a buyer is underwriting a residential or hotel conversion instead of another office lease-up. A structural engineer needs to sign off on that before it goes on an identification list, not after.

The Capitol Hill government district sits just east of the main office towers, the State Capitol building, the City and County Building, and a cluster of state and county agency offices. Buildings leasing to state government inside that district tend to run long-term, low-turnover leases, and a buyer comparing a downtown office deal to a suburban one should factor that credit stability into the underwriting rather than treating every downtown lease the same.

sections.heading: What Actually Trades Downtown
sections.html:
The realistic property types coming out of downtown Denver right now are:

  • Class A and B high-rise office towers, some full, some half-empty
  • ground-floor retail and restaurant space along the 16th Street corridor
  • parking structures serving the office and stadium crowd
  • older office buildings being pitched as residential or hotel conversions
  • government-leased buildings with long-term single-tenant credit

sections.heading: 16th Street Mall and the Transit Crowd
sections.html:
The 16th Street corridor has been torn up and rebuilt in phases, new pavers, new lighting, new bus lanes, and that construction has hurt ground-floor retail leasing along the mall for a stretch of years running. A tenant on a percentage-rent lease down there has taken a real hit during construction blocks, and a buyer needs trailing sales figures, not a pro forma, before trusting that rent roll.

Union Station sits at the north end of downtown and pulls commuter rail, light rail, and Amtrak into one building. Retail and hospitality space immediately around the station has leased at a premium to the rest of downtown because of that foot traffic, and it is worth treating as its own micro-market rather than lumping it in with the office towers six blocks south.

sections.heading: Diligence a Downtown Buyer Skips at Their Own Risk
sections.html:
Parking ratio is the first thing to check on any downtown office building. A tower built in 1985 was not designed for today's parking expectations, and a shortfall shows up fast once a tenant starts comparing it to a suburban DTC lease with a surface lot out front. Conversion feasibility studies, if a seller is marketing the building on that story, need an independent engineer's review rather than the seller's consultant deck alone. And any building inside a downtown historic district faces design review on exterior changes, which slows a renovation timeline more than buyers expect coming from the suburbs.

Elevator and vertical transportation modernization is another cost buyers underestimate on a 1970s or 1980s tower. A full elevator bank upgrade runs into real money, and it's the kind of capital item that shows up on an engineering report rather than a rent roll. Any skybridge or shared-easement connection between adjacent buildings also needs its own title review, since those agreements sometimes run with a prior owner rather than the property itself.

sections.heading: Positioning a Downtown Identification
sections.html: Downtown Denver office rarely stands alone on an identification list right now given the vacancy overhang. Investors coordinating a 1031 into this submarket typically pair a downtown tower or ground-floor retail parcel with a DTC office asset or a LoDo mixed-use building as backups, since both offer a different risk profile if the downtown deal falls through in diligence. A qualified intermediary should have the identification paperwork ready before the 45-day window gets tight, because downtown deals with government or credit tenants tend to move slower through lender underwriting than a straightforward suburban net lease.

faqs.q: Is downtown Denver office a reasonable 1031 replacement property right now?
faqs.a: It can be, but go in with eyes open on vacancy. A fully-leased Class A tower with government or law-firm tenants underwrites very differently than a half-empty Class B building being pitched as a turnaround.

faqs.q: What is driving office-to-residential conversion talk downtown?
faqs.a: Persistent vacancy in the older towers and a housing shortage in the core have made conversion pencil out for some buildings. It only works on floor plates that can actually take a residential layout, so get an engineer's opinion before assuming a building qualifies.

faqs.q: Does the 16th Street Mall construction affect retail leases along the corridor?
faqs.a: Yes. Ground-floor tenants on percentage rent have seen real sales drops during construction phases. Pull trailing twelve-month sales figures instead of relying on a pre-construction pro forma.

faqs.q: How does a government tenant change underwriting on a downtown building?
faqs.a: Government leases bring long-term credit stability but often move slower through renewal and buildout approvals. A lender familiar with GSA or state lease structures will underwrite it faster than one that only handles private-sector credit.

faqs.q: Can a downtown Denver identification stand on its own for the three-property rule?
faqs.a: It usually shouldn't given current vacancy. Most buyers pair a downtown asset with a DTC office building or a LoDo property as backups so the exchange doesn't collapse if the downtown deal falls apart in diligence.
